newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - U.K. watchdog examines sickly petrol market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.K. watchdog examines sickly petrol market.

text.p: A regulatory investigation into prices being charged by large multinational corporations normally centres on how consumers are being cheated.
In Britain, where the Office of Fair Trading announced on Tuesday a periodic review of the retail petrol market, it's quite the opposite.
Cheaper pump prices are the focus of a periodic review announced by the OFT.

The Director General of Fair Trading, John Bridgemann, said the review was already underway and he would decide by autumn whether the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) needed to take further action.

The newly elected Labour government said before it took power in May that it was sympathetic to a review of practices in the petrol retail sector, where cut-throat price competition forced 10 percent of retailers out of business last year.
The decision comes nearly one year after a parliamentary trade committee issued recommendations to soften the impact of a nation-wide price war that shut 1,500 petrol stations last year.
Esso's Pricewatch campaign, launched in early 1996 promising to match its lowest-priced competitors, and aggressive pricing by the supermarkets were blamed for the competitive retail petrol market.

"We are examining the effects of changes in the market's structure since the MMC report of 1990," Bridgemann said in a statement. "This will, of course, include the move of supermarkets into petrol retailing and the effect of this on other outlets."
Independent retailers welcomed the investigation while other industry analysts said the government was unlikely to take any intervention that would artificially lift prices.
"My initial reaction is that it's about time and it's long overdue," said James Frost, chairman of Save Group Plc, the largest independent retailer in Britain with 614 sites.

"The reality is that you've got multinational corporations who have got different pockets from which to pluck their money and therefore they have been supporting unprofitable downstream activities from upstream activities," he added. "In my mind that is unfair trading."
The government should legislate that oil companies cannot sell petrol below a benchmark price that is based on the spot wholesale market, he said.

"The difficulty with consumers is they want their cake today and tomorrow," he said. "It is not going to be long before the only sites they will be able to buy petrol at are a supermarket or one of the major oil companies and then the price will rocket."
Oil Price Assessments Ltd (OPAL) estimated that gross petrol margins in Britain for unleaded petrol were 4.4 pence per litre as of last Friday, in the basement of European rankings.
"Quite frankly, as far as pump prices are concerned, I don't think consumers have had it so good for so long," said Robert Olle, a director of OPAL. "Why should (the government) want to change that?"
Substantial involvement by the government would be viewed as intervention, which it may not want, he added.

"Nothing is going to change as far as what is happening on the streets," said Stephen Brooks, a consultant at Wood Mackenzie in Edinburgh. "As long as Esso continues its Pricewatch campaign then prices will remain under pressure and margins will be under pressure."

"The financial situation is not looking that good for the petrol retailing industry this year," he said. "While it's not as bad as 1996, it's certainly not as good as it needs to be for operators to make an acceptable return on investment."
